name: Oh Hell
description: Oh Hell (also known as Oh Hell!) is a classic trick-taking card game that emphasizes precision bidding over raw power. Unlike most trick-takers where you try to win as many tricks as possible, the goal is to win exactly the number of tricks you bid. It is famous for its 'River' structure, where hand sizes increase and decrease throughout the game, and its 'Hook' rule that prevents every player from being successful simultaneously.

overview.description: Oh Hell (also known as Oh Hell!) is a classic trick-taking card game that emphasizes precision bidding over raw power. Unlike most trick-takers where you try to win as many tricks as possible, the goal is to win exactly the number of tricks you bid. It is famous for its 'River' structure, where hand sizes increase and decrease throughout the game, and its 'Hook' rule that prevents every player from being successful simultaneously.

history.origins: Believed to have originated in the early 20th century (likely New York clubs), it is a member of the 'Bid Whist' and 'Skat' family but simplified for social play.
timeline: 1936: Listed in official card game manuals as 'Oh Well!'.
1950s: Becomes a staple of 'College Card Games' under many names (Oh Pshaw, Blackout).
Present: One of the most common introductory games for competitive bidding logic.
history.cultural: Known by dozens of local names: Up and Down the River, Estimation, 10-Down, and German Bridge.
history.evolution: The game's name was frequently censored to 'Oh Well' or 'Oh Heck' in family editions.

setup.players: From 3 to 7 people can play. The game is best when played with 4 to 6.
setup.deck: 52 cards. Rank: A > K > Q > J > 10... > 2.
setup.dealing: Varies by round. Round 1: 1 card each. Round 2: 2 cards each. (Ascending up to 10 or 12, then descending back to 1).

rules.objective: Score the most points by winning EXACTLY the number of tricks you bid.
rules.gameplay: Play starts with the player to the dealer's left leading any card. Players must follow suit if able; otherwise they may play any card including trump. Highest trump wins the trick, or if no trump was played, highest card of the led suit wins. The trick winner leads to the next trick; play continues until all tricks are complete.
keyRules: Bid the exact number of tricks you will take; scoring only for making the bid exactly.
Follow suit if able; if void, may play any card including trump.
Trump is determined by the card turned after the deal; highest trump or highest of led suit wins the trick.
The Hook: dealer may not bid so that total bids equal the number of tricks in the hand.
Hand sizes follow the River: start at 10 (or 8/7 by player count), decrease to 1, then increase back.

strategy.basic: In a 1-card round, if you have a high trump (Ace or King), bid 1; otherwise, bid 0. As the hand size grows, evaluate your 'Safe Tricks' (Aces/Kings in short suits) and your 'Danger Tricks' (Queens/Jacks) which might win unexpectedly.
strategy.intermediate: The 'Zero Bid' Defense: If you bid zero, your goal is to discard high cards as early as possible on other people's tricks. If you have a King and someone leads that suit, throw it on! Don't get stuck with high cards in the final tricks when you have no other choice but to win.
strategy.advanced: Social Manipulation (The Undercut): If the bids are 'Under' (total bids < tricks available), someone will be forced to win a trick they didn't want. Use this. If you bid 1 and you've already won your trick, start leading low cards in your long suits to force the opponents who wanted 0 tricks to win them.
tips: If you are the dealer and the total bids are currently equal to the tricks, you ARE 'The Hooked'. You must bid something else, forcing the table into unbalanced territory.
Don't bid 1 with a 'middling' card like a 7 or 8 unless it is a trump and the hand size is large.

variations.name: Sequence of hands
variations.description: Some play 1 up to max then down to 1; some start at max and go down then up (e.g. 7-1-7 or 10-1-10). Maximum cards per hand may be 7, 10, 12, or 13 depending on player count and variant.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: River sequence and max hand size depend on house rules; add overrides when mapping to engine constants.

variations.name: Determining trumps
variations.description: When all cards are dealt there is no card to turn; hand is played at no trump. Some use a fixed rotation of trump suits (e.g. spades, diamonds, clubs, hearts) or include no-trump in the sequence.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Trump rotation or no-trump would require engine.trumpConfig overrides when implemented.

variations.name: Hook and bidding style
variations.description: Some play without the Hook (dealer may bid so total equals tricks). Some use simultaneous bidding (fists on table, reveal on count) instead of turn-based.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Hook and bidding style would override engine.trickConfig.bidding when implemented.

scoring.description: 10 points bonus for making your bid + 1 point per trick taken. If you miss your bid, you get 0 points (or 1 point per trick with no bonus).
scoring.winCondition: Score the most points by winning EXACTLY the number of tricks you bid.
